variants.name: Hand-written guard over rusqlite
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's database crates deliberately stop short of an ORM concurrency token: with rusqlite the guarded statement itself reports the outcome - Connection::execute returns the number of rows changed (and Connection::changes() reads the count of the most recent statement) - while sqlx exposes the same figure as rows_affected on its query result. The pattern is therefore the hand-written version column plus a dedicated conflict error variant, so a stale write cannot be ignored at the call site.
pitfalls: Connection::changes() is connection-scoped state: any other statement executed before it is read (logging, a dropped transaction guard) overwrites the count.
rusqlite connections are not Sync - sharing one across threads needs a pool or mutex, and a per-statement pooled connection breaks the one-system-transaction rule.
Discarding the returned row count (let _ = ...) makes the conflict invisible; model it as a #[must_use] result or an error variant.

variants.name: In-process CAS retry loop
variants.implementation_notes: In-process the same mechanics are std atomics: load the current version, compute the new value, and publish it with compare_exchange (or compare_exchange_weak inside a loop); a failure yields the current value, which the caller re-reads and recomputes. This is the hardware form of validate-then-act and the basis of Rust's lock-free data structures; it does not persist anything, so an edit session that outlives the process still needs a stored token.
pitfalls: Relaxed ordering gives the exchange but not the happens-before edge needed to publish the data the version guards; Acquire/Release is the minimum.
compare_exchange compares bit patterns, so packing payload and version into one atomic only works if the type is Copy with no padding-induced duplicate representations.
Spinning on compare_exchange_weak under real contention burns a core - add backoff or fall back to a lock.
